title: Yesterday I went
goal: Talk about what has happened, use the past tense for every person, and negate it correctly.
bekal: form the fi'il maaḍi for eight persons
tell what you did yesterday, step by step
use *kaana* for nominal sentences in the past

dialogs.title: حِوَار — كَيْفَ كَانَتْ عُطْلَتُكَ؟
dialogs.intro: Monday morning on campus. Laila asks Budi about his weekend.

lines.speaker: بُودِي:
lines.id: I left on Friday by train.

lines.speaker: بُودِي:
lines.text: زُرْتُ الْمَكْتَبَةَ الْقَدِيمَةَ، وَأَكَلْتُ سَمَكًا عَلَى الْبَحْرِ.

lines.text: إِنْ شَاءَ اللهُ نُسَافِرُ مَعًا الْمَرَّةَ الْقَادِمَةَ.

notes: **The past tense uses ENDINGS, not prefixes.** It is the reverse of the present: ذَهَبْتُ (I went), ذَهَبْتَ (you went), ذَهَبَ (he went), ذَهَبْنَا (we went). The front stays the same; the tail changes.

**The most basic form is "he".** ذَهَبَ means "he went" — and that is the form dictionaries use. So when a dictionary lists كَتَبَ, it literally says "he wrote", not "to write". The habit is surprising at first, then starts to make sense.

**كَانَ fills the "to be" gap in the past.** A nominal sentence needs no verb in the present, but in the past it does: أَنَا مَشْغُولٌ (I'm busy) → كُنْتُ مَشْغُولًا (I was busy). Notice that the description takes fathah after كَانَ.

**كَانَتْ عُطْلَتُكَ — the verb comes before its subject.** The most typically Arabic order is **[verb] + [subject] + [the rest]**. English puts the subject first; Arabic doesn't always. Both orders are correct, but verb-first sounds more formal.

**Negating the past: مَا or لَمْ.** مَا خَرَجْتُ and لَمْ أَخْرُجْ both mean "I didn't go out". The difference: مَا + past verb (more everyday), لَمْ + **present** verb with a sukun on the end (more formal, more common in writing).
**وَحْدَكَ — "alone".** It changes with the person: وَحْدِي (I alone), وَحْدَكِ (you, f., alone), وَحْدَهُ (he alone).

**صَدِيقَيْنِ — the dual, as an object.** The dual has two shapes: صَدِيقَانِ when it is the subject, صَدِيقَيْنِ when it is an object or after a preposition. Same pattern as غُرْفَتَانِ / غُرْفَتَيْنِ.

grammars.title: Fi'il maaḍi — the past tense
after: These endings are **exactly the same for every verb** — no exceptions, and no middle vowel to guess as in the present. The past tense is actually the easiest part of the Arabic verb.
Notice that ـتُ (I) and ـتَ (you) differ by just one vowel at the end. In fast speech the difference is subtle, and context helps.

grammars.title: كَانَ — "was"
after: Notice that the description takes **fathah** after كَانَ: هُوَ طَالِبٌ → كَانَ طَالِبًا. This is one place where case endings are really heard and really used.
كَانَ is also used with a present verb for past habits: كُنْتُ أَدْرُسُ فِي جَاكَرْتَا ("I used to study in Jakarta").

sections.title: Verbs you'll use for telling stories

blocks.text: Some of the verbs above have a middle ا that changes: زَارَ becomes زُرْتُ (not زَارْتُ), كَانَ becomes كُنْتُ, قَالَ becomes قُلْتُ. These are "hollow" verbs, and the pattern is fixed: **the middle letter drops out as soon as the ending starts with a consonant.**

blocks.title: Past time expressions
items: أَمْسِ (yesterday) · أَوَّلَ أَمْسِ (the day before yesterday) · اَلْأُسْبُوعَ الْمَاضِيَ (last week) · اَلشَّهْرَ الْمَاضِيَ (last month) · اَلسَّنَةَ الْمَاضِيَةَ (last year) · قَبْلَ يَوْمَيْنِ (two days ago) · مُنْذُ سَنَتَيْنِ (two years ago).
Notice that اَلْمَاضِي means "past, gone by" and agrees with its noun like any adjective — including taking اَلْ.

blocks.text: Both are correct and both are used. The one thing to remember: **لَمْ can never be followed by a past verb.** لَمْ ذَهَبْتُ is an error that gets noticed at once; the right form is لَمْ أَذْهَبْ, with the present verb and a sukun on the end.

blocks.title: Four negators, one table
items: **لَيْسَ** — sentences with no verb: لَيْسَ هٰذَا كِتَابِي.
**مَا / لَمْ** — past verbs: مَا ذَهَبْتُ / لَمْ أَذْهَبْ.
**لَنْ** — the future: لَنْ أَذْهَبَ ("I won't go"), covered in unit 17.

exercises.prompt: Put into the past tense to match the subject.

items: Yesterday I went to the market.

exercises.prompt: Negate in two ways (مَا and لَمْ).
Tell about your last weekend in six past-tense sentences.

answers: ذَهَبْتُ — كَتَبَ — دَرَسَتْ — أَكَلْنَا — عَمِلُوا — شَرِبْتِ
أَمْسِ ذَهَبْتُ إِلَى السُّوقِ. — رَجَعْنَا يَوْمَ الْجُمُعَةِ. — هِيَ مَا خَرَجَتْ مِنَ الْبَيْتِ. — كَانَتِ الْعُطْلَةُ مُمْتَازَةً. — كُنْتُ مَشْغُولًا. — زَارُوا الْمَتْحَفَ.
مَا ذَهَبْتُ / لَمْ أَذْهَبْ — مَا أَكَلَ / لَمْ يَأْكُلْ — مَا كَتَبَتْ / لَمْ تَكْتُبْ — مَا رَجَعْنَا / لَمْ نَرْجِعْ — مَا فَهِمُوا / لَمْ يَفْهَمُوا

Example: أَمْسِ ذَهَبْتُ إِلَى بُوغُور — سَافَرْتُ يَوْمَ السَّبْتِ بِالْقِطَارِ — ذَهَبْتُ مَعَ عَائِلَتِي — زُرْنَا الْحَدِيقَةَ الْكَبِيرَةَ — أَكَلْنَا سَمَكًا فِي مَطْعَمٍ صَغِيرٍ — رَجَعْنَا فِي الْمَسَاءِ
